items.title: Developers mixing Claude Code and Codex in shared setups
facts: Developers are mixing Claude Code and Codex instead of picking one today.
A poll asks how people split the work: one plans and one codes, switch when a limit hits, run the same task in both, or something else.

x_posts.author: @AGTPinsights
x_posts.text:
Developers are mixing Claude Code and Codex instead of picking one today. Here's what you need to know.

This follows the rush to free tools like OpenCode and T3 Code, as Claude usage limits frustrate paying users. The question now is how to run two coding agents side by side.

A poll asks how people split the work: one plans and one codes, switch when a limit hits, run the same task in both, or something else. One developer moved everything into a single VS Code setup with Claude Code, Codex, skills and tools via MCP or CLI. That way a new model gets tested inside the same setup. Another says running both in separate windows is the caveman way.

The pushback on T3 Code, the free app that drives both from one place: one user says Codex isn't as bad as it's made out to be, and T3 Code isn't as good as claimed. They plan to go back to using Codex and Claude Code separately.

Codex limits split opinion. One long-time Plus user says limits are at their worst yet, with about 3 to 4 times more usage a year ago, and that was before the 5-hour limits. One user says they left Codex because of limits and went all-in on Claude. Another says Codex limits are now insanely good.

On the model side, OpenAI lists GPT-5.3 Codex API pricing at $1.75 per million input tokens and $14 per million output tokens.

Key numbers:
- 2 agents, Claude Code and Codex, used together
- 4 ways to split the work in the poll
- $1.75 input and $14 output per million tokens for GPT-5.3 Codex
- 3 to 4x more Codex usage a year ago, per one Plus user

The takeaway: with limits shifting on both sides, devs are building setups that can switch between Claude Code and Codex.

items.title: Developer shares detailed AGENTS.md to reduce AI comment slop
facts: Do not write comments unless they are absolutely necessary to explain some very complex business logic or used as an input for tools to read and act on.
The point of this rule is to keep out AI slop comments. AI writes way too many and way too verbose comments.

x_posts.author: @xodud_rkd
x_posts.text:
My AGENTS.md

Do not write comments unless they are any of:

- absolutely necessary to explain some very complex business logic (in which case, keep it concise and clear)
- used as an input for tools to read and act on. For example:
  - entries in `.git-blame-ignore-revs` saying which commit is excluded from git blame
  - a lint or type checker suppression with a concise reason when introducing a truly unavoidable violation
- a TODO or FIXME
  - Not great to have those, but if it's unavoidable, make sure to include a strong, concise reason for why it's there or, better yet, link to a GitHub issue for the follow-up work

Explanation: The point of this rule is to keep out AI slop comments. AI writes way too many and way too verbose comments. Code comments are, in a way, a violation of DRY code. You must update logic in two locations to change the code, and "hard to change" is literally the definition of tech debt. We should instead aim to write code that is intuitive and clear, even at a glance, to the reader, being both easy to maintain and high performance

Don't assume that the existing code is correct or the right way of doing things / good coding patterns. In fact, there are a lot of bad coding practices, overly complex code, code smells, etc. If something doesn't look right, speak up. Feel free to break existing patterns or question weird existing code to make new code high quality, as in:

- correct
- secure
- performant
- readable
- easy to maintain/change
- modern

In descending order of importance

Pre-merge tests are one fast safety net run with `make test-fast` inside a 60 second budget, plus a small service suite run with `make test-service` for behavior that needs real PostgreSQL or Valkey. The allowlists live in `scripts/test-fast.sh` and `scripts/test-service.sh`, and the full rules live in `tests/README.md`. When adding new features inside the allowlist, add meaningful tests there. Don't add tests that don't check anything substantial. I'd rather…

items.title: Community shares multi-model Claude Code setup with Sonnet, Haiku, and Opus advisor
facts: Run Sonnet 5.5 for the session and writes the code, Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel, Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls.
Opus only steps in at three moments: before a plan locks, when the same error shows up twice, and before calling it done.

x_posts.author: @hayatomaruu
x_posts.text:
THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING TREASURE

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

"Rebuild my Claude Code setup around this tree:
1. Run the main session on Sonnet 5.5 with Opus 5.5 as advisor.
2. Create three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), docs (pulls the API reference).
3. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before locking a plan, after the same error twice, and before calling a task done.
4. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

↳ http://code.claude.com/docs/en/advisor

save this, then read the full guide for Opus 5.5 loop + jev engineering ↓

items.title: OpenAI acquiring Pierre Computer Company to integrate code storage into Codex
facts: OpenAI announced November 4 it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, the startup behind Code Storage and the open-source Trees and Diffs libraries that already render file browsing and change review inside the Codex app.
The plan, once the deal closes: fold Code Storage into Codex, so the agent that writes your code also has somewhere to keep it.

x_posts.author: @TommyBeFamous
x_posts.text:
OpenAI just bought the plumbing under Codex.

@OpenAI announced November 4 it will acquire Pierre Computer Company, the startup behind Code Storage and the open-source Trees and Diffs libraries that already render file browsing and change review inside the Codex app.

The plan, once the deal closes: fold Code Storage into Codex, so the agent that writes your code also has somewhere to keep it. From the first branch an agent creates to code being deployed, in OpenAI's own framing.

Two days before the announcement, OpenAI's engineering team explained why. Agent traffic had pushed its own Git backend, Pando, below 90% reliability, and they rebuilt it. This acquisition is the other half of that story.

No price disclosed. No closing date. The companies stay separate until regulatory approvals land, and Code Storage customers keep using the service meanwhile. Pierre's open-source projects stay open source.

I read this as OpenAI saying the quiet part out loud... Codex is not a coding assistant anymore. It is becoming the whole shop. Git hosting included.

items.title: Advice against treating AI coding agents like junior developers
facts: Don't slow down your agents. Don't treat them like junior devs. Approving every small step.
My agents still don't push code. They plan, write, file issues and ask questions. A human decides what ships.

x_posts.author: @madsonmac
x_posts.text:
Don't slow down your agents

Don't treat them like junior devs

Approving every small step

Rewriting their plans

Checking every line like it's their first week

Your AI model read Clean Code

It read Clean Architecture

It read almost everything we read, and a lot more

I'm a software engineer since 2003 and I still have to remind myself of this

The model often knows more than I do about how to write the code

So give it more autonomy

But not zero control

My agents still don't push code

They plan, write, file issues and ask questions

A human decides what ships

Autonomy inside the work

A human at the boundary

If you review everything, you are the bottleneck
